an7.49:4.3: It’s like a chicken’s feather or a scrap of sinew thrown in a fire. It shrivels up, shrinks, rolls up, and doesn’t stretch out.
an7.49:4.4: In the same way, when a mendicant often meditates with a mind reinforced with the perception of death, their mind draws back from desire to be reborn. They shrink away, turn aside, and don’t get drawn into it. And either equanimity or revulsion become stabilized.
an7.49:5.1: If a mendicant often meditates with a mind reinforced with the perception of death, but their mind is drawn to desire to be reborn, and not repulsed,
an7.49:5.2: they should know: ‘My perception of death is undeveloped. I don’t have any distinction higher than before. I haven’t attained a fruit of development.’
an7.49:5.3: In this way they are aware of the situation.
an7.49:5.4: But if a mendicant often meditates with a mind reinforced with the perception of death, their mind draws back from desire to be reborn. They shrink away, turn aside, and don’t get drawn into it. And either equanimity or revulsion become stabilized,
an7.49:5.5: they should know: ‘My perception of death is well developed. I have realized a distinction higher than before. I have attained a fruit of development.’
an7.49:5.6: In this way they are aware of the situation.
an7.49:5.7: ‘When the perception of death is developed and cultivated it’s very fruitful and beneficial. It has freedom from death as its objective and culmination.’
